text.p: World commodity prices mostly ended a dull week little changed on Friday but crude oil prices took a hammering late on Friday largely on extended profit-taking in the London futures market ahead of a long holiday weekend, traders said.
London October futures for international benchmark Brent crude closed at $20.41 a barrel, down 31 cents on the day.
Earlier the contract traded close to four-month highs, propped up by rising demand for energy ahead of the northern hemisphere winter.
"It's extended profit-taking and weakness in the crude," a floor broker said.

A flood of North Sea physical cargoes which appeared on the market on Friday combined with economics which made it too expensive to ship crude oil across the Atlantic to the huge U.S. market led to a sharp fall on the spot market.
However Brent is averaging $2 a barrel more than 1995's $16.94, defying analysts' expectations that a surge in supplies would outweigh extra demand.
They cited stronger-than-expected demand growth for oil products this year from China, other Asian nations, Latin America and the United States.
The industrial metals on the London Metal Exchange had an uncertain week with the flagship copper contract trading in a narrow range between $1,900 and $1,970 per tonne.
Copper was helped higher on Friday by book-squaring ahead of a three-day British holiday weekend.
Traders said bouts of short covering lifted copper from a low of $1,932 to $1,949, a $14 gain from Thursday, but the market never seriously attempted to break from its range.
Talk that Egypt may be in the market late Friday or over the weekend for U.S. wheat boosted CBOT wheat futures to a higher close, traders said.
After the close it was confirmed Egypt was seeking 50,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat for September or October shipment.
Support also may have come from hopes for U.S. wheat business with China this year.
Wheat closed two to four cents per bushel higher, with September up 2-1/4 at $4.52-3/4.
Wheat futures volume was estimated at 13,000, up from 9,648 Thursday, according to the CBOT.
CSCE world sugar futures closed barely budged from opening levels, as producer selling and trade buying framed the day's activity.
After trading slightly lower for most of the session, the October contract slipped over unchanged on light trade buying in the afternoon, but promptly fell back.
The benchmark October contract settled unchanged at 11.85, having ranged from 11.87 to 11.79. March ended 0.01 higher at 11.46, while the back months finished flat to 0.06 higher.
London white sugar futures ended slightly firmer. October settled 70 cents higher to $352.40 while December closed unchanged at $345.90.
New York precious metals futures ended mostly firmer Friday, on low volumes, with trading expected to remain slow next week due to holidays in London and Hong Kong on Monday.
COMEX December gold ended up $0.70 an ounce at $392.2 an ounce, after trading up to a high for the week at $393.7.
Total estimated gold futures volume was 13,000 lots.
In New York bullion trade, spot gold was quoted $388.00/388.50, from a London afternoon fix of $387.50, and a New York close Thursday at $387.20/387.70.
Last trades or bids for key Australian-interest commodities.
